nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Common Name: Spanish Mackerel
Scientific Name: Scomberomorus maculatus

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum: Chordata
	Class:	Osteichthyes
	Order:	Perciformes
	Family: Scombridae

Other Common Names:  mackerel (664); spotted Spanish mackerel (791); horse mackerel, bay mackerel, Spaniard, spotted cybium (195 560).

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  Prized commercial species, most fishing occurs along the south Atlantic coast from Cape Hatteras, North Carolina to the Florida Keys, and in the eastern Gulf from the Florida Keys to the Mississippi River delta (481 194 571 731 690 360 203 536 791).  Commercial landings for the U.S. in 1987 were 6,838,000 pounds of which 2,258,000 were landed 0-3 mi offshore and 4,580,000 were landed 3-200 mi offshore (513).  Florida produces over 90% of commercial catch while landings in Texas are less than 2,000 pounds (194 238 327 731).  Florida commercial landings totaled 3,701,776 lbs worth $1.57 million in 1989 (902).  Main fishing areas in Florida are in the Florida Keys and in the Atlantic between Palm Beach and Cape Canaveral (238).  Principle commercial gear used are run around gill nets and purse seines, with some hook and line catches, but in Mississippi most of commercial catch comes from shrimp trawl catches in offshore waters (47 382 690 731 791).  Marketed mostly fresh or frozen (791).

Recreational: An important gamefish along the Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico prized for both its fighting ability and high quality as a food fish (47 194 203 327 360 382 481 571 690 731).  The most productive recreational fishing area is along the Atlantic coast from Cape Hatteras, North Carolina to the Florida Keys, followed by the eastern Gulf of Mexico from the Keys to the Mississippi River, and then from the Mississippi River to the Mexican border in waters < 3 mi. from shore.  The 1990 sport catch of Spanish mackerel has been estimated as 294,000 fish (1363).  Principle fishing method is hook and line while trolling or drifting, with some catches in Florida made from boats, piers, bridges, jetties, and beaches by casting, live bait fishing, jigging, and drift fishing (536 731 788 791).

Ecological Role: A predominantly piscivorous carnivore.

Indicator: This species has been used by NMFS to study heavy metal contamination (457).  A potential exists for damage by oil pollution to eggs and larvae present near the water surface (419).

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  Atlantic coast from Cape Cod in the Gulf of Maine to Miami; in the Gulf of Mexico from the Florida Keys to the Yucatan Peninsula, Mexico (128 129 200 203 238 571 690 791); occasionally occurs at Bermuda (891 932), and absent from Barbados and the Antilles except Cuba and Haiti (788).  A summer visitor all along the Atlantic coast of the U.S. as far north as New York occurring less regularly along the southern coasts of New England.  Occasionally strays into the colder waters of the Gulf of Maine with a single report occurring from Maine (51).  Center of abundance appears to be Atlantic coast of Florida (194 203 731).  Populations of the Gulf of Mexico and Atlantic may comprise two distinct stocks (360).

Within the study area: Seasonally abundant in the coastal waters of both coasts of Florida with areas of concentration off Cape Romano on the Gulf coast, from Palm Beach to Cape Canaveral on the Atlantic coast, and off Key West (238).  Large schools are common in fall and winter off south Florida, an area considered to be their major wintering ground (238 690).

Mobility and Migration:

nodes.title: Life Mode
nodes.body: Pelagic and schooling (47 116 223 238 302 481 571 590 791 932). Prefer neritic waters (382 571).  Activity and feeding appears to be evenly distributed between day and night (481 702 786).

nodes.title: Movement/Migrations
nodes.body: Seasonally migratory; little information is known other than movements are ambicoastal corresponding to water temperature, and depending on water temperature, can be quite extensive (571 481 47).  Three major migration routes are hypothesized: along the Mexico-Texas coast; along the northern Gulf of Mexico coast and west coast of Florida; along the Atlantic coast (360).  In the eastern Gulf, these fish move northward in the Gulf during late winter and spring appearing off the central west coast of Florida about the first of April (481 690).  Movements continue westward and terminate along the northern Gulf coast.  In the fall, migration is back to the south to the wintering grounds in south Florida waters (481 690).  The major wintering grounds are off Florida, but some fish overwinter in the Campeche-Yucatan area (360 690).  Fish are caught throughout the year indicating some fish move offshore during cold weather and do not migrate (116 481 550).

nodes.title: Substrate
nodes.body:
Young mackerel seem to prefer clean sand (47), but preferences for other life stages of this pelagic fish have not been recorded.

Larvae: Occur most frequently offshore over inner shelf (12-34 m) in polyhaline to euhaline waters (449 450 774) during the summer months (36 194 322 40 1372).  Abundance appears to be greatest in the northeastern gulf (419).  Houde et al (1372) found larvae to be relatively common along the entire Florida Gulf coast with most occurrences at stations <20 m deep.  Most frequent collections of larvae made in water depths ranging 5.0-12.8 m, but larvae have been found as deep as 91.5 m (194 424).

Juveniles: Found offshore and in beach surf, sometimes reported from lower river outflows, estuaries, sounds, bays, lagoons, and marshes, but are generally not considered estuarine dependent (47 116 194 223 255 419 449 583 584 694 774 786).  Occur in oligohaline to euhaline salinities, but appear to prefer euhaline water (116 194 223 255 449 583).  Most juveniles are collected at 9.1-18.3 m, but collection depths can range from the surface down to 91.5 m (194 223).  Some juveniles apparently use estuaries as nursery grounds (238).

Adults: Typically found offshore in neritic waters and along coastal areas usually near barrier islands and particularly their passes; frequent shallower depths and are seldom found deeper than 73.2 m (116 195 223 255 302 382 560 590 664).  In Florida majority inhabit coral reefs, off-shore currents, and tide rips of clear tropical waters (382 481 1394).  Adults are seldom taken near river mouths or in low salinity waters (195), but one study from Florida reports that they enter rivers on flood tides to feed on shrimp migrating seaward (702).  Will enter estuaries and bays especially high salinity areas during seasonal migrations, but are considered rare and infrequent (571 583 651 382 786 47 538 560 791 932).  Collected from salinities ranging from oligohaline to euhaline with an apparent preference for euhaline waters (116 194 223 255 449 583).

nodes.title: Temperature
nodes.body:
Larvae: Found in the northwestern Gulf of Mexico from 19.6-29.8 C; preferences of 21-27 C and 20.2-29.8 C reported (47 449). Found in coastal waters of the Florida panhandle from 28.4-30.5 C (194).

Juveniles/adults: Juveniles occur over a temperature range of 10-34.9 C (116 194 223 255 548 550).  Occasional appearance in bays seems to be limited to waters above 24 C (786), and is most abundant in samples collected at 25 C or higher (550).  Adults reported to occur over a range of 20-32 C and to seldom enter waters below 18 C (195 225 255 664 789).  Reported to prefer temperatures of 21-27 C (195).  Distribution is apparently governed primarily by water temperature (238 1394), with the northern range defined by the 20 C isotherm (1394 1395).  Reported to be killed at several Florida locations by low temperatures caused by freezes (236 836 1023 1068).

nodes.title: Salinity
nodes.body:
Larvae: Collected in a salinity range of 28.3-37.4 ppt (47 194 449 450) and are most abundant at 28.3-34.4 ppt (449).

Juveniles/adults: Most juveniles found in salinities exceeding 10 ppt (550 694 47), but they can occur over a range of 0.21 to 37.4 ppt (374 188 550 694 223 116 194 548 936).  Adults are generally associated with marine salinities (225 664).  Reported from 14.5-36.7 ppt in Texas and Florida (255 789).  One fish 245 mm TL was collected in a Texas river in 17.2 ppt (80).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Reproductive Mode: Separate sexes. Oviparous; reproduction by externally broadcast sexual products.

Mating/Spawning: Active and ripening oocytes present throughout spring and summer from April through mid-September in Florida, with spawning probably occurring June through September (481 382 571).  Some spawning may occur in April or October and year-round spawning is considered possible in Florida (215).  The onset of spawning generally progresses from south to north (238).  Spawning can occur during the day but is primarily at night, with multiple spawnings possible over a prolonged season (47 195 382 424 571 613 834).  Spawning takes place in inner shelf waters usually inside the 20m depth contour (194 450 1372), and possibly in the vicinity of barrier islands and passes at depths of 12-18 m.  Spawning also occurs occasionally over the mid and outer shelf possibly as deep as 200 m (47 449).  Spawning temperatures range from 21 to 31 C, but are usually in excess of 22 C and seldom below 18 C (47 322).  Salinities for spawning range from 30 to 36.5 ppt (47 322).  Peak spawning seems to be during June through August with the eastern and northeastern Gulf of Mexico probably the most important spawning area (449 481 382).

Fecundity: Fish in south Florida are sexually mature in their second or third year of life when they are about 250-350mm FL (238 382).  Powell (571) considered previous studies to have overestimated age by one year; therefore maturity may occur in fish less than 1 year (571).  Many age 1 fish observed had ripe oocytes, but examinations made of these fish during the spawning season suggested eggs were not advanced enough to be spawned that season (571).  Spanish mackerel probably do not become fully mature until age 2 with the bulk of the spawning population composed of fish age 3 and older (419 571).  Fecundity increases with length and weight (238 195).  Fecundity has been estimated as 1.5 million eggs for a 2.7 kg female while a 0.45 kg fish had an estimated 300,000 eggs (195).  Fecundity ranges from 100,000 to 2,000,000 eggs for fish ranging 295 to >2,415 g (312 mm to 626 mm FL) (215).  Sturm (1396) reported lower fecundity rates for fish collected in Trinidad, ranging from 26,057 to 149,736 eggs per female for fish from 490 to 645mm.  Gesteira (1397) reported a mean fecundity of 2,204,000 ova per female for fish collected in Brazil.

Gesteira (1397) presented the following fecundity equations for length, weight, and age based on 47 mature females from Brazil:

[eq]
     F = (-3.273 + 95 FL) x 10^3
     F = (-241 + 1.452 W) x 10^3
     F = (-300 + 443 A) x 10^3
[/eq]

Godcharles and Murphy (238) presented the following fecundity equations from unpublished data of Finucane and Collins based on 11 females:

[eq]
     F = 9.076 x 10^2 (W^0.919)     r^2 = 0.941
     F = 1.027 x 10^-2 (FL^2.863)    r^2 = 0.925
[/eq]

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Egg:  Eggs are buoyant, transparent and smooth with a single oil droplet 0.25 mm in diameter.  Eggs are round in shape and 0.91-1.15 mm in diameter (613 195 47).  Perivitelline space is approximately 0.1 mm across.  Hatching is primarily during summer months and occurs about 15.5 hours after fertilization at 29 C, and 25 h after fertilization at 26 C (225 314 449 834).

Larvae: Larval stage lasts from 2.56-13.5 mm TL (225).  Larvae are 2.56 mm TL or 2.0 mm SL at hatching and attain 2.8 SL within 3 days (225 449 613).  Larvae in the wild reported to range from 1.6 to 11.8 mm SL (424).  Yolk sac absorbed by 3.18 mm TL on about the fourth day (613 774).

Juvenile: Juveniles range 13.5-225.0 mm Tl in size (314 774).  Using otolith data, Klima (382) reported that for both sexes combined, length increased about 18.4 cm in the first year, 13.8 cm in the second year, 14.0 cm in the third year, 10.1 cm in the fourth year and 1.4 cm in the fifth year.  Females mature at a length between 250 and 320 mm and males between 280 and 340 mm (382).  The majority of spawners are age 2 or age 3 fish >350mm FL (295 571).

Adult: Adult growth is rapid until year 5 in females and year 6 in males and then slows appreciably (203). Equations expressing the fork length-standard length relationship for both sexes combined were calculated by Powell (571) using data from 135 males and 217 females:

[eq]
      FL = 1.0728(SL) + 2.4267
      SL = 0.9321(FL) - 2.2619
[/eq]

The equations for the length-weight relationship calculated by Powell (571) are:

[eq]
      Males:   W = 1.1519 x 10^-5 (SL^2.9822)
      Females: W = 4.7491 x 10^-6 (SL^3.1373)
     Combined: W = 9.9632 x 10^-6 (SL^3.0070)
[/eq]

Von Bertalanffy growth equations based on annuli readings from otoliths have been calculated by several authors (203 295 571 1396 1398).  There is disagreement in the early literature about interpretation of annuli data, resulting in differences in age determinations and yielding different growth estimates.  Powell (571) noted discrepancies between the average length at age reported by Klima (382) and his own data.  Powell (571) concluded that the age determinations of Klima (382) based on otolith data were in error, and were off by one year due to incorrect reading of the first annulus (i.e. all of Klima's  fish were actually 1 year younger than the age he assigned to them).  A similar situation may explain the differences between the equations of Powell and those of Sturm (1396) given below.

Fable et al (203) attempted to resolve the conflicts, and examined 1,929 specimens from four US coastal states including Texas, Mississippi, Louisiana, Florida, and Georgia.  They presented the following growth equations:

Florida fish:

[eq]
        Males:  FL = 776(1 - e^(-0.27(t + 0.73)))
       Females: FL = 731(1 - e^(-0.38(t + 0.73)))
[/eq]

All areas combined:

[eq]
        Males:  FL = 794{1 - e^(-0.24(t + 0.94))}
       Females: FL = 739{1 - e^(-0.33(t + 0.99))}
[/eq]

They felt that these equations were more accurate than those of Powell (571) because they included the oldest fish in their calculations, whereas Powell only included fish up to 5 years old.

Powell (571) presented the following growth equations:

[eq]
      Males:  L = 515(1 - e^(-0.48(t + 1.12)))
     Females: L = 645(1 - e^(-0.45(t + 0.78)))
[/eq]

The equations of Helser and Malvestuto (295) from otolith data for 223 male and female Spanish mackerel are:

[eq]
      Males:  FL = 552(1 - e^(-0.29 (t + 1.66)))
     Females: FL = 604(1 - e^(-0.45 (t + 0.75)))
[/eq]

Sturm (1396) used otolith data from 817 fish (303 male, 514 female) from Trinidad and presented the following growth equations:

[eq]
      Males:  L = 710(1 - e^(-0.26(t + 0.73)))
     Females: L = 830(1 - e^(0.23(t + 0.94)))
[/eq]

Females reach up to 802 mm FL and grow faster than males which have been recorded up to 723 mm FL (203 128).  The maximum reported weight is 11 kg (560 457 47).  Maximum size reported by Robins et al (788) as 830 mm and 5 kg.  It is believed that most females live longer than males (203).  Maximum life spans reported for Spanish mackerel have been 9 years for females and 7 years for males (203).

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body:
Larvae/juveniles:  Larval and post-larval Spanish mackerel are primarily piscivorous.  Finucane et al (1128) found fish in the stomachs of all 307 specimens they examined; carangids, clupeids and engraulids occurred frequently in the stomachs of fish ranging from 2.8 to 20.0 mm SL.  Invertebrates occurred only infrequently, with nudibranch larvae (the most common invertebrate type) present in only 2% of the guts.  The diet of 489 juveniles also consisted primarily of fish, with engraulids constituting the dominant prey item in both number and volume (1128).  Squid, although only a minor component of the juvenile diet (2% of volume), was the dominant invertebrate consumed (1128).  Juveniles from the Gulf of Mexico consumed a greater variety of prey items than juveniles collected from the Atlantic coast.

Adults:  Fast moving surface feeder, primarily piscivorous, which preys heavily on schooling fishes in the families Clupeidae, Carangidae, and Engraulidae (238 419 617).  Klima (382) found that 76% of the 109 stomachs he examined contained clupeid fish remains.  Squid, crabs, and shrimp are also components of the diet in Texas (47 376 560 590 617).  Engraulids are also a very important food item accounting for as much as 99% of the volume and 98% of the number of food items in both the Gulf and the Atlantic (238 540).

nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body:
Predation: This species is a major prey item of sharks (Carcharhinus leucas, C. obscurus, Sphyrna zygaem, Lamna nasas, Galeoceido cuvieri) and dolphins (Tursiops truncatus) (376 419).
Parasites/Diseases:  Berrien and Finan (1394) presented an extensive list of parasites which occur on Spanish mackerel and noted that no diseases or abnormalities have been reported.

sections.heading: HEADER
sections.content:
Title: Spanish Mackerel (Scomberomorus maculatus)

FLELMR Code:  1970

sections.heading: TAXONOMY
sections.content:
Common Name: Spanish Mackerel
Scientific Name: Scomberomorus maculatus

sections.heading: Classification
sections.content:
Phylum: Chordata
	Class:	Osteichthyes
	Order:	Perciformes
	Family: Scombridae

Other Common Names:  mackerel (664); spotted Spanish mackerel (791); horse mackerel, bay mackerel, Spaniard, spotted cybium (195 560).

sections.heading: VALUE & STATUS
sections.content:
Commercial:  Prized commercial species, most fishing occurs along the south Atlantic coast from Cape Hatteras, North Carolina to the Florida Keys, and in the eastern Gulf from the Florida Keys to the Mississippi River delta (481 194 571 731 690 360 203 536 791).  Commercial landings for the U.S. in 1987 were 6,838,000 pounds of which 2,258,000 were landed 0-3 mi offshore and 4,580,000 were landed 3-200 mi offshore (513).  Florida produces over 90% of commercial catch while landings in Texas are less than 2,000 pounds (194 238 327 731).  Florida commercial landings totaled 3,701,776 lbs worth $1.57 million in 1989 (902).  Main fishing areas in Florida are in the Florida Keys and in the Atlantic between Palm Beach and Cape Canaveral (238).  Principle commercial gear used are run around gill nets and purse seines, with some hook and line catches, but in Mississippi most of commercial catch comes from shrimp trawl catches in offshore waters (47 382 690 731 791).  Marketed mostly fresh or frozen (791).

Recreational: An important gamefish along the Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico prized for both its fighting ability and high quality as a food fish (47 194 203 327 360 382 481 571 690 731).  The most productive recreational fishing area is along the Atlantic coast from Cape Hatteras, North Carolina to the Florida Keys, followed by the eastern Gulf of Mexico from the Keys to the Mississippi River, and then from the Mississippi River to the Mexican border in waters < 3 mi. from shore.  The 1990 sport catch of Spanish mackerel has been estimated as 294,000 fish (1363).  Principle fishing method is hook and line while trolling or drifting, with some catches in Florida made from boats, piers, bridges, jetties, and beaches by casting, live bait fishing, jigging, and drift fishing (536 731 788 791).

Ecological Role: A predominantly piscivorous carnivore.

Indicator: This species has been used by NMFS to study heavy metal contamination (457).  A potential exists for damage by oil pollution to eggs and larvae present near the water surface (419).

sections.heading: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
sections.content:
Overall:  Atlantic coast from Cape Cod in the Gulf of Maine to Miami; in the Gulf of Mexico from the Florida Keys to the Yucatan Peninsula, Mexico (128 129 200 203 238 571 690 791); occasionally occurs at Bermuda (891 932), and absent from Barbados and the Antilles except Cuba and Haiti (788).  A summer visitor all along the Atlantic coast of the U.S. as far north as New York occurring less regularly along the southern coasts of New England.  Occasionally strays into the colder waters of the Gulf of Maine with a single report occurring from Maine (51).  Center of abundance appears to be Atlantic coast of Florida (194 203 731).  Populations of the Gulf of Mexico and Atlantic may comprise two distinct stocks (360).

Within the study area: Seasonally abundant in the coastal waters of both coasts of Florida with areas of concentration off Cape Romano on the Gulf coast, from Palm Beach to Cape Canaveral on the Atlantic coast, and off Key West (238).  Large schools are common in fall and winter off south Florida, an area considered to be their major wintering ground (238 690).

Mobility and Migration:

sections.heading: Life Mode
sections.content: Pelagic and schooling (47 116 223 238 302 481 571 590 791 932). Prefer neritic waters (382 571).  Activity and feeding appears to be evenly distributed between day and night (481 702 786).

sections.heading: Movement/Migrations
sections.content: Seasonally migratory; little information is known other than movements are ambicoastal corresponding to water temperature, and depending on water temperature, can be quite extensive (571 481 47).  Three major migration routes are hypothesized: along the Mexico-Texas coast; along the northern Gulf of Mexico coast and west coast of Florida; along the Atlantic coast (360).  In the eastern Gulf, these fish move northward in the Gulf during late winter and spring appearing off the central west coast of Florida about the first of April (481 690).  Movements continue westward and terminate along the northern Gulf coast.  In the fall, migration is back to the south to the wintering grounds in south Florida waters (481 690).  The major wintering grounds are off Florida, but some fish overwinter in the Campeche-Yucatan area (360 690).  Fish are caught throughout the year indicating some fish move offshore during cold weather and do not migrate (116 481 550).

sections.heading: Substrate
sections.content:
Young mackerel seem to prefer clean sand (47), but preferences for other life stages of this pelagic fish have not been recorded.

Larvae: Occur most frequently offshore over inner shelf (12-34 m) in polyhaline to euhaline waters (449 450 774) during the summer months (36 194 322 40 1372).  Abundance appears to be greatest in the northeastern gulf (419).  Houde et al (1372) found larvae to be relatively common along the entire Florida Gulf coast with most occurrences at stations <20 m deep.  Most frequent collections of larvae made in water depths ranging 5.0-12.8 m, but larvae have been found as deep as 91.5 m (194 424).

Juveniles: Found offshore and in beach surf, sometimes reported from lower river outflows, estuaries, sounds, bays, lagoons, and marshes, but are generally not considered estuarine dependent (47 116 194 223 255 419 449 583 584 694 774 786).  Occur in oligohaline to euhaline salinities, but appear to prefer euhaline water (116 194 223 255 449 583).  Most juveniles are collected at 9.1-18.3 m, but collection depths can range from the surface down to 91.5 m (194 223).  Some juveniles apparently use estuaries as nursery grounds (238).

Adults: Typically found offshore in neritic waters and along coastal areas usually near barrier islands and particularly their passes; frequent shallower depths and are seldom found deeper than 73.2 m (116 195 223 255 302 382 560 590 664).  In Florida majority inhabit coral reefs, off-shore currents, and tide rips of clear tropical waters (382 481 1394).  Adults are seldom taken near river mouths or in low salinity waters (195), but one study from Florida reports that they enter rivers on flood tides to feed on shrimp migrating seaward (702).  Will enter estuaries and bays especially high salinity areas during seasonal migrations, but are considered rare and infrequent (571 583 651 382 786 47 538 560 791 932).  Collected from salinities ranging from oligohaline to euhaline with an apparent preference for euhaline waters (116 194 223 255 449 583).

sections.heading: Temperature
sections.content:
Larvae: Found in the northwestern Gulf of Mexico from 19.6-29.8 C; preferences of 21-27 C and 20.2-29.8 C reported (47 449). Found in coastal waters of the Florida panhandle from 28.4-30.5 C (194).

Juveniles/adults: Juveniles occur over a temperature range of 10-34.9 C (116 194 223 255 548 550).  Occasional appearance in bays seems to be limited to waters above 24 C (786), and is most abundant in samples collected at 25 C or higher (550).  Adults reported to occur over a range of 20-32 C and to seldom enter waters below 18 C (195 225 255 664 789).  Reported to prefer temperatures of 21-27 C (195).  Distribution is apparently governed primarily by water temperature (238 1394), with the northern range defined by the 20 C isotherm (1394 1395).  Reported to be killed at several Florida locations by low temperatures caused by freezes (236 836 1023 1068).

sections.heading: Salinity
sections.content:
Larvae: Collected in a salinity range of 28.3-37.4 ppt (47 194 449 450) and are most abundant at 28.3-34.4 ppt (449).

Juveniles/adults: Most juveniles found in salinities exceeding 10 ppt (550 694 47), but they can occur over a range of 0.21 to 37.4 ppt (374 188 550 694 223 116 194 548 936).  Adults are generally associated with marine salinities (225 664).  Reported from 14.5-36.7 ppt in Texas and Florida (255 789).  One fish 245 mm TL was collected in a Texas river in 17.2 ppt (80).

sections.heading: REPRODUCTION
sections.content:
Reproductive Mode: Separate sexes. Oviparous; reproduction by externally broadcast sexual products.

Mating/Spawning: Active and ripening oocytes present throughout spring and summer from April through mid-September in Florida, with spawning probably occurring June through September (481 382 571).  Some spawning may occur in April or October and year-round spawning is considered possible in Florida (215).  The onset of spawning generally progresses from south to north (238).  Spawning can occur during the day but is primarily at night, with multiple spawnings possible over a prolonged season (47 195 382 424 571 613 834).  Spawning takes place in inner shelf waters usually inside the 20m depth contour (194 450 1372), and possibly in the vicinity of barrier islands and passes at depths of 12-18 m.  Spawning also occurs occasionally over the mid and outer shelf possibly as deep as 200 m (47 449).  Spawning temperatures range from 21 to 31 C, but are usually in excess of 22 C and seldom below 18 C (47 322).  Salinities for spawning range from 30 to 36.5 ppt (47 322).  Peak spawning seems to be during June through August with the eastern and northeastern Gulf of Mexico probably the most important spawning area (449 481 382).

Fecundity: Fish in south Florida are sexually mature in their second or third year of life when they are about 250-350mm FL (238 382).  Powell (571) considered previous studies to have overestimated age by one year; therefore maturity may occur in fish less than 1 year (571).  Many age 1 fish observed had ripe oocytes, but examinations made of these fish during the spawning season suggested eggs were not advanced enough to be spawned that season (571).  Spanish mackerel probably do not become fully mature until age 2 with the bulk of the spawning population composed of fish age 3 and older (419 571).  Fecundity increases with length and weight (238 195).  Fecundity has been estimated as 1.5 million eggs for a 2.7 kg female while a 0.45 kg fish had an estimated 300,000 eggs (195).  Fecundity ranges from 100,000 to 2,000,000 eggs for fish ranging 295 to >2,415 g (312 mm to 626 mm FL) (215).  Sturm (1396) reported lower fecundity rates for fish collected in Trinidad, ranging from 26,057 to 149,736 eggs per female for fish from 490 to 645mm.  Gesteira (1397) reported a mean fecundity of 2,204,000 ova per female for fish collected in Brazil.

Gesteira (1397) presented the following fecundity equations for length, weight, and age based on 47 mature females from Brazil:

[eq]
     F = (-3.273 + 95 FL) x 10^3
     F = (-241 + 1.452 W) x 10^3
     F = (-300 + 443 A) x 10^3
[/eq]

Godcharles and Murphy (238) presented the following fecundity equations from unpublished data of Finucane and Collins based on 11 females:

[eq]
     F = 9.076 x 10^2 (W^0.919)     r^2 = 0.941
     F = 1.027 x 10^-2 (FL^2.863)    r^2 = 0.925
[/eq]

sections.heading: Length Range
sections.content:
Egg:  Eggs are buoyant, transparent and smooth with a single oil droplet 0.25 mm in diameter.  Eggs are round in shape and 0.91-1.15 mm in diameter (613 195 47).  Perivitelline space is approximately 0.1 mm across.  Hatching is primarily during summer months and occurs about 15.5 hours after fertilization at 29 C, and 25 h after fertilization at 26 C (225 314 449 834).

Larvae: Larval stage lasts from 2.56-13.5 mm TL (225).  Larvae are 2.56 mm TL or 2.0 mm SL at hatching and attain 2.8 SL within 3 days (225 449 613).  Larvae in the wild reported to range from 1.6 to 11.8 mm SL (424).  Yolk sac absorbed by 3.18 mm TL on about the fourth day (613 774).

Juvenile: Juveniles range 13.5-225.0 mm Tl in size (314 774).  Using otolith data, Klima (382) reported that for both sexes combined, length increased about 18.4 cm in the first year, 13.8 cm in the second year, 14.0 cm in the third year, 10.1 cm in the fourth year and 1.4 cm in the fifth year.  Females mature at a length between 250 and 320 mm and males between 280 and 340 mm (382).  The majority of spawners are age 2 or age 3 fish >350mm FL (295 571).

Adult: Adult growth is rapid until year 5 in females and year 6 in males and then slows appreciably (203). Equations expressing the fork length-standard length relationship for both sexes combined were calculated by Powell (571) using data from 135 males and 217 females:

[eq]
      FL = 1.0728(SL) + 2.4267
      SL = 0.9321(FL) - 2.2619
[/eq]

The equations for the length-weight relationship calculated by Powell (571) are:

[eq]
      Males:   W = 1.1519 x 10^-5 (SL^2.9822)
      Females: W = 4.7491 x 10^-6 (SL^3.1373)
     Combined: W = 9.9632 x 10^-6 (SL^3.0070)
[/eq]

Von Bertalanffy growth equations based on annuli readings from otoliths have been calculated by several authors (203 295 571 1396 1398).  There is disagreement in the early literature about interpretation of annuli data, resulting in differences in age determinations and yielding different growth estimates.  Powell (571) noted discrepancies between the average length at age reported by Klima (382) and his own data.  Powell (571) concluded that the age determinations of Klima (382) based on otolith data were in error, and were off by one year due to incorrect reading of the first annulus (i.e. all of Klima's  fish were actually 1 year younger than the age he assigned to them).  A similar situation may explain the differences between the equations of Powell and those of Sturm (1396) given below.

Fable et al (203) attempted to resolve the conflicts, and examined 1,929 specimens from four US coastal states including Texas, Mississippi, Louisiana, Florida, and Georgia.  They presented the following growth equations:

Florida fish:

[eq]
        Males:  FL = 776(1 - e^(-0.27(t + 0.73)))
       Females: FL = 731(1 - e^(-0.38(t + 0.73)))
[/eq]

All areas combined:

[eq]
        Males:  FL = 794{1 - e^(-0.24(t + 0.94))}
       Females: FL = 739{1 - e^(-0.33(t + 0.99))}
[/eq]

They felt that these equations were more accurate than those of Powell (571) because they included the oldest fish in their calculations, whereas Powell only included fish up to 5 years old.

Powell (571) presented the following growth equations:

[eq]
      Males:  L = 515(1 - e^(-0.48(t + 1.12)))
     Females: L = 645(1 - e^(-0.45(t + 0.78)))
[/eq]

The equations of Helser and Malvestuto (295) from otolith data for 223 male and female Spanish mackerel are:

[eq]
      Males:  FL = 552(1 - e^(-0.29 (t + 1.66)))
     Females: FL = 604(1 - e^(-0.45 (t + 0.75)))
[/eq]

Sturm (1396) used otolith data from 817 fish (303 male, 514 female) from Trinidad and presented the following growth equations:

[eq]
      Males:  L = 710(1 - e^(-0.26(t + 0.73)))
     Females: L = 830(1 - e^(0.23(t + 0.94)))
[/eq]

Females reach up to 802 mm FL and grow faster than males which have been recorded up to 723 mm FL (203 128).  The maximum reported weight is 11 kg (560 457 47).  Maximum size reported by Robins et al (788) as 830 mm and 5 kg.  It is believed that most females live longer than males (203).  Maximum life spans reported for Spanish mackerel have been 9 years for females and 7 years for males (203).

sections.heading: FOOD HABITS
sections.content:
Larvae/juveniles:  Larval and post-larval Spanish mackerel are primarily piscivorous.  Finucane et al (1128) found fish in the stomachs of all 307 specimens they examined; carangids, clupeids and engraulids occurred frequently in the stomachs of fish ranging from 2.8 to 20.0 mm SL.  Invertebrates occurred only infrequently, with nudibranch larvae (the most common invertebrate type) present in only 2% of the guts.  The diet of 489 juveniles also consisted primarily of fish, with engraulids constituting the dominant prey item in both number and volume (1128).  Squid, although only a minor component of the juvenile diet (2% of volume), was the dominant invertebrate consumed (1128).  Juveniles from the Gulf of Mexico consumed a greater variety of prey items than juveniles collected from the Atlantic coast.

Adults:  Fast moving surface feeder, primarily piscivorous, which preys heavily on schooling fishes in the families Clupeidae, Carangidae, and Engraulidae (238 419 617).  Klima (382) found that 76% of the 109 stomachs he examined contained clupeid fish remains.  Squid, crabs, and shrimp are also components of the diet in Texas (47 376 560 590 617).  Engraulids are also a very important food item accounting for as much as 99% of the volume and 98% of the number of food items in both the Gulf and the Atlantic (238 540).

sections.heading: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
sections.content:
Predation: This species is a major prey item of sharks (Carcharhinus leucas, C. obscurus, Sphyrna zygaem, Lamna nasas, Galeoceido cuvieri) and dolphins (Tursiops truncatus) (376 419).
Parasites/Diseases:  Berrien and Finan (1394) presented an extensive list of parasites which occur on Spanish mackerel and noted that no diseases or abnormalities have been reported.
